articles.title: Smaller pie, firmer grip
articles.content: WHEN railways and factories began transforming 19th-century Europe, the rulers of the Habsburg Empire understood their economic potential. Yet they resisted industrialisation. Friedrich von Gentz, Metternich’s adviser, explained why: “We do not desire at all that the great masses shall become well-off and independent.” His reasoning ended with a revealing question: “How could we otherwise rule over them?” The Habsburg rulers were not necessarily ignorant of the economic benefits of technological progress. They feared its political consequences. A more prosperous society might also become more independent, weakening their grip on power. This historical episode helps explain a persistent puzzle in Pakistan: why do those in power repeatedly choose institutions (rules of the game) and policies that constrain economic progress, even when they too benefit from better alternatives? The answer may lie in the distinction between economic and political returns. Elites do not necessarily choose arrangements that maximise national income, or even their own immediate economic gains. They also consider how a change might affect their ability to retain power and capture future returns — what we call the political replacement effect in economics. Technological and institutional changes can expand economic opportunities while simultaneously creating new centres of political power. Incumbents may, therefore, resist changes that threaten their hold on power. The calculation is straightforward. A reform may make the economy larger and even increase the income of existing elites. But if it also raises the probability of their political displacement, or reduces the share of future gains they can command, their expected returns may decline. Under these conditions, elites may rationally prefer an inferior arrangement that preserves their political dominance. In other words, a smaller pie under a secure scenario may be more attractive than a larger pie with uncertain future distribution. An economically promising change can redistribute political power. Pakistan’s recent history offers three institutional and technological choices that are especially revealing. First is local government. The Constitution requires provinces to devolve political, administrative and financial authority to elected local representatives. Yet successive governments have either delayed local elections or weakened the institutions they create. The largest province, Punjab, last held LG elections a decade ago. Other provinces have also adopted various approaches to limit devolution. KP, for example, recentlyincreased the population thresholdfor village and neighbourhood councils to reduce the number of councils, potentially weakening representation. In Sindh, transfers to LGs declined from 15.7 per cent of provincial general revenue receipts to just 5.8pc in the 2025-26 budget. What makes these choices economically questionable? Elected LGs with genuine fiscal and administrative authority can better respond to local needs, improve service delivery, and strengthen accountability. Why, then, resist them? Because empowered LGs also create political competitors. A mayor controlling development funds and public services can build an independent political constituency. Legislators lose influence over resources that help sustain their electoral networks. Even if improved local governance generates greater prosperity, its political dividends may accrue to someone else. The second example is fiscal federalism. The seventh NFC award raised provinces’ share of the divisible pool to 57.5pc, with constitutional protection against subsequent reductions. But since then, the federal government has built a parallel fiscal system undermining the very principle of federalism. Petroleum levy collections, which are not shared with provinces, reached Rs1.567 trillion in 2025-26. Provinces were also asked to generate surpluses and, lately, to provide grants to the federal government. The parallel system may be responding to genuine fiscal pressures, but it preserves fiscal discretion at the centre, despite the constitutional commitment to provincial autonomy. In essence, after the seventh NFC, the provincial share fell without anyone touching the award. The political economy consideration here is that meaningful fiscal autonomy changes the distribution of power. Provinces with independent revenue sources and predictable resources can pursue their own priorities and strengthen their political standing. But the provinces are no different. While demanding autonomy from Islamabad, they resist transferring meaningful authority and resources to elected LGs. At each tier, those holding resources resist passing them down. The third example concerns technology: rooftop solar. Faced with high electricity tariffs, the public began investing in their own power generation. Solar offered consumers cheaper electricity, greater reliability, and reduced dependence on the national grid. Yet policy increasingly moved towards discouraging its adoption. The government not only imposed a 10pc sales tax on solar panels but, in February, it replacednet metering with net billingfor new connections, substantially lowering the compensation for surplus electricity supplied to the grid. A more economically sustainable response would have restructured costly contractual obligations, modernised the grid, and established fair charges for network use. Why has such adjustment proved so difficult? One explanation is that decentralised electricity generation threatens more than power producers’ revenues. It also weakens an established system through which economic resources, contracts, subsidies, and regulatory discretion are concentrated. These instruments carry financial and political value. Reforming them could improve overall economic performance while reducing the influence of those who currently control them. These three cases are not identical, but they share a key feature: an economically promising change can redistribute political power, creating incentives for incumbents to resist or dilute it. This is what makes the political replacement argument more powerful than the familiar explanation that elites protect their economic rents. Sometimes they may sacrifice economic gains, including their own, to preserve the political position from which future gains can be secured. The implication is that Pakistan’s development problem cannot be resolved through better policy advice alone. The harder challenge is creating institutions that reduce the ability of those in power to obstruct changes that might eventually displace them. The stakes extend beyond the current examples. AI is creating new opportunities while challenging existing economic and political hierarchies. Whether or not Pakistan embraces those opportunities will depend largely on how it responds to a technology most capable of redistributing power. Until the existing calculations change, the country may continue choosing a smaller pie for the sake of a firmer grip. The writer is an associate professor of economics at the Lahore School of Economics.
articles.author: Waqar Wadho

articles.title: FCC on workplace harassment
articles.content: THE commentary that followed the recent Federal Constitutional Court (FCC)judgementdismissing the harassment claim of an NBP employee gives the impression that the court has rolled back the scope of the workplace harassment law so that it now covers only incidents of an overtly sexual nature, excluding conduct that amounts to gender-based discrimination. This is incorrect. The correct position of the law now is this: allegations of workplace harassment prior to 2022 (which is when the Protection Against Harassment of Women in the Workplace Act was amended) must involve conduct of an overtly sexual nature to fall within the scope of the law. Actions that take place after the 2022 amendment are covered by the law not only if they are overtly sexual in nature, but also if they are rooted in gender-based discrimination. Let’s see why. First, let’s look at the definition of ‘harassment’. Prior to January 2022, it was defined to cover “any unwelcome sexual advance, request for sexual favours or other verbal or written communication or physical conduct of a sexual nature or sexually demeaning attitudes, causing interference with work performance or creating an intimidating, hostile, or offensive work environment, or the attempt to punish the complainant for refusal to comply to such a request or is made a condition for employment”. This definition was amended in January 2022 by adding the following: “discrimination on basis of gender, which may or may not be sexual in nature, but which may embody a discriminatory and prejudicial mindset or notion, resulting in discriminatory behaviour on basis of gender against the complainant” (Section 2[h][ii] of the Act). The court interpreted the original definition restrictively, following the reasoning of the first Nadia Naz judgement. The amendment was made after the 2021 Supreme Court decision inNadia Naz vs President of Pakistan. This case, which analysed and applied the original, pre-2022 definition of harassment, concluded that the law only covers harassment of an overtly sexual nature. The 2022 amendment, passed a few months after the judgement, rectified the limitation in the original definition as interpreted by the Supreme Court in the Nadia Naz judgement of 2021. The amended definition explicitly includes gender-based discrimination within the meaning of harassment. The amended definition would not apply retrospectively. The expanded definition, which broadens the scope of the actionable wrong, would only cover actions that take place after the amendment. But in 2023 the Supreme Court, reviewing the Nadia Naz judgement, held that the original definition was broad enough to include gender-based discrimination. Harassment as originally defined should be interpreted to include conduct that is not overtly sexual in nature but amounts to gender-based discrimination. The Supreme Court declared that the bench’s interpretation of the original definition was too restrictive. The interpretation in the Nadia Naz judgement on review would be brilliant were it not for the 2022 amendment. By interpreting the original definition to have essentially the same meaning and effect as the 2022 insertion, the Supreme Court implies that the 2022 amendment was redundant. This contradicts a basic principle of statutory interpretation, which requires that each statutory provision should be interpreted to give it a distinct meaning. It may well be that the 2022 amendment was not needed because the original definition should be interpreted as broadly and purposively as the Supreme Court did in the Nadia Naz judgement on review. But when the legislature amended the definition in 2022 to explicitly cover gender-based discrimination, it also implied that the earlier definition was restrictive, which is why the amendment was needed. By explicitly expanding the definition, it endorsed the view that the original definition did not cover gender-based discrimination. The FCC in its recent judgement did the same. The FCC interpreted the original definition restrictively, following the reasoning of the first Nadia Naz judgement. It did not refer to the 2022 amendment, and it did not need to because the incidents involved in the case predated the amendment. The amended definition would not apply to these facts. It would have been more edifying if the FCC had clearly explained this, but lucid, well-written judgements are unfortunately uncommon. Let’s say, as many have argued, that the FCC should have interpreted the original definition more broadly to include gender-based discrimination. What implication would that have for the current definition of harassment? Such an interpretation would entail that the second part of the definition is redundant because the first part covers conduct embodying gender-based discrimination. Such reasoning would again contradict the principle of statutory interpretation, which says that the legislature does not waste its words. The FCC decision is deeply flawed, but for another reason. The FCC has not applied its own interpretation properly. The harassment at issue in this case was overtly sexual in nature. The evidence put forward at the earlier stages of the case, before the Islamabad High Court and the ombudsperson, shows that the complainant faced harassment that was unambiguously sexual. It is disturbing that the FCC did not consider this conduct to fall within the scope of the original definition. Flawed as it is, the FCC has not overruled the 2022 amendment to the law. The expanded definition (Section 2(h)(ii)) still stands, but it will only apply to incidents that took place or are alleged to have taken place after the date of the amendment. Prior incidents will be covered by the original definition, which will be interpreted restrictively. This clarification is important because after the FCC ruling and the outrage against it, many potential claimants believe that the pervasive gender-based discrimination they currently face at the workplace is not covered by the law. People sitting on workplace harassment committees have told me that their mandate is now restricted to only incidents that are overtly sexual in nature. We must remind them that it is not. The writer is a lawyer and the author of Progressive Laws In Patriarchal Societies.
articles.author: Sara Malkani

articles.title: Lucky draw
articles.content: EVERY Ramazan, the scene repeats itself. The sun sets, the fast is broken, the studio lights come up. Hundreds of people in their brightest clothes wave placards and wait to be chosen. On one side of the stage, a row of motorbikes gleams. On the other, cars sit under sponsors’ banners. The host strides out, the crowd roars, and the games begin. Answer a riddle. Recite a tongue twister. Squash a mango into your face, etc. If you are lucky, and loud enough, you go home with a motorbike. In 2013, you might have gone home with a baby. That Ramazan, the show’s host Aamir Liaquat Hussain handed abandoned infants to screened, childless couples live on TV, between the phones and the land deeds. He insisted it was best for the children. Perhaps it was, but the ratings showed what the show was really for. We have been watching this for more than a decade. The late Hussain launched the format of Ramazan shows in 2012, and Dawn reported in 2017 that networks earned up to Rs500,000 a minute in ad breaks. Asked why poor winners got luxury cars they couldn’t afford to run, he said they “will be able to sell them”. I thought of those shows when a wedding in Sialkot turned deadly. The groom was Ansar Mehmood, a TikToker known to his over 800,000 followers as Mr Patlu. Police claim the organisers had advertised the event on social media with prize draws for motorcycles, cars, and other valuables. A large crowd gathered at a cricket ground and then an announcement over the loudspeaker asked everyone to enter the ground at once. Perhaps it is time to ask what we have been watching all along. Two people were killed. Many were injured. Six people have been arrested, and, at the time of writing, the TikToker had secured bail. It would be easy to treat this as a freak accident, or to blame one careless influencer and move on. But the Sialkot wedding is not an aberration. It is the logical next step of a culture we built on television and have now handed to the internet. The game shows taught us that prizes draw crowds, and crowds draw ratings. Social media has learned the same lesson, and stripped away whatever restraint television had. A TV studio has a set capacity, security staff, producers, and, in theory, a regulator watching. A TikTok giveaway has none of these. An influencer with a phone can summon thousands of people to a field with a single video, promise them a motorbike, and bear no responsibility for what happens when they arrive. Giveaways are a standard tool of the attention economy. Brands use them, influencers use them, and the logic is simple: offer something for free and the followers come. Most of the time, the cost is a few likes and a lost afternoon. But that Saturday, the cost was casualties. The more uncomfortable question, though, is not about the influencer. It is about the crowd. Why would so many people go to a stranger’s wedding on the chance of winning a prize? Because, for many of them, a motorbike is not a toy. It is a commute. It is a job on a delivery app. It is the difference between a son getting to college and staying home. In a country where wages have barely kept pace with prices, a lucky draw is not a game. It is a lottery ticket out. That is what Hussain understood when he gave away cars he knew winners would sell. The prize was never really the car. It was the money, the escape, the small chance of a better month. Our game shows made entertainment out of that hope. Now our influencers have made a business model out of it. None of this excuses the organisers. Running an event for thousands of people without proper permits, planning or crowd control is negligence. But arrests will not touch the deeper incentive. As long as hope is cheap and attention is profitable, someone will keep dangling the motorbike. So what would change it? Clearer rules on public giveaways would help, and so would treating large influencer events like any other public gathering, with permits and safety checks. Platforms could take some responsibility for promotions that draw crowds into unsafe spaces. But the harder change is the one no regulator can make. We have spent years cheering as people humiliate themselves for prizes on our screens. We have laughed at the scramble. We have made it a Ramazan tradition. Perhaps it is time to ask what we have been watching all along. Not a game, but a country telling us how badly it needs a lucky draw. Postscript: As readers pointed out, the Women on Wheels programme began in Punjab in 2016, a fact my last column inadvertently omitted to mention. The writer is a journalist who conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: Midterm surprise
articles.content: THAT the Republican Party would lose the midterm elections for the US Congress was never in doubt. It was its overwhelming defeat that surprised everyone. Democrats have attained a clear majority in the 100-member US Senate (54 Democrats, 44 Republicans) and a massive lead in the 435-member House of Representatives (253 Democrats, 157 Republicans). What explains this major shift? One plausible answer is the Iran war and its effects on gas prices, inflation, and the higher cost of living. Importantly, America’s younger population never owned this war. It has been widely seen as Israel’s war that America was fighting. Vice President J.D. Vance has rightly concluded that “the reason we lost [in the elections] is the war”. Even Donald Trump acknowledged that the war with Iran was a factor, though he defended its objectives. While the Iran war and its side effects may have been the main reason for the Republicans’ defeat, several other factors also weighed in. In his election campaigns, Trump had opposed distant wars, yet he entered into one with Iran at the behest of Israel. American voters saw this as a clear repudiation of the ‘America First’ approach that Trump had touted in his speeches. It was hard for Americans to accept America’s subordination to Israeli interests. This, in turn, raised questions about US legislators’ links with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, whose activities are aligned closely with the agenda of a foreign government (Israel), Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and US complicity by continuing to provide weapons and assistance to Israel. All this did not sit well with young Americans. How will it impact America’s foreign policy? Two aspects merit attention. First, Trump is unlikely to resume the war with Iran or follow through on his threats to use the mother of all bombs against Iran. The reason is clear. His Republican Party will not want a return to a war that is so unpopular with Americans. A return to war could jeopardise the party’s future stakes, including the race for the White House. In fact, America would like to see an honourable exit from the war. The answer lies in diplomacy and a return to the Islamabad MoU, which meets both the key US demand that Iran should not produce nuclear weapons and the Iranian demand that economic sanctions be lifted and Iran’s frozen assets released. This provides an honourable off-ramp to both sides to end a war that serves no one but Israel. As for the Strait of Hormuz, everyone wants it to reopen fully because disrupted supplies of oil, gas, petroleum products, and fertilisers have been hurting the world economy. To that end, America should end its naval blockade, and Iran should agree not to interrupt shipping in the strait. All these points have been amply covered in the Islamabad MoU. The parties to the Makkah Agreement — Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye — have a special role. They must increase their diplomatic efforts, as should Qatar and Oman. Even China and Russia may need to step in to help find a diplomatic solution. China, in particular, has an interest in ensuring fuel supplies and the smooth functioning of markets. The window of opportunity may be limited, as the caretaker Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, might plan some manoeuvre, a false flag operation, or some drastic action like using a tactical nuclear weapon to force Iran to respond and then rope the US into the war with Iran. Republicans will not want to return to a war unpopular with Americans. The second aspect of US foreign policy relevant to us is whether it will affect Pakistan-US ties. The latter have always been transactional and viewed through America’s own geopolitical interests. As of now, post-Marka-i-Haq Pakistan continues to enjoy respect as a stabilising force in the region. Further, given that Afghanistan is once again becoming a safe haven for the world’s terrorist organisations, Pakistan’s geopolitical importance as the only state fighting terrorism in all its forms, including proxy terrorism by India from Afghanistan, will remain valid. Pakistan has flourishing bilateral trade with the US, along with cooperation in multiple areas, including agriculture and IT. Relations between Pakistan and the US are, thus, likely to continue at their own pace. Although many in the ranks of the Democrats tend to have pro-Israel, pro-India, anti-Iran, and anti-China sentiments — similar to the Republicans — American foreign policy will remain a major subject of discussion in the Democrats-dominated Congress in the months ahead. Transatlantic alliances, relations with Canada, adventures like Venezuela, opposition to climate change, tariff wars, Islamophobia, subservience to Israeli interests, and Trump’s refusal to regulate AI technologies could all be up for review when the re-composed Congress starts its work next January. The writer is a former foreign secretary of Pakistan.
articles.author: Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry

articles.title: Trump’s choice
articles.content: ALTHOUGH American President Donald Trump has admitted that the disastrous Iran war was a factor in theheavy drubbinghis party received from the Democrats in the midterm polls, there are few indications he has decided to wind down the conflict. In fact, Mr Trump hassent mixed messages, saying there has been “progress” in talks with Iran, while also threatening to “destroy what is left” of the Islamic Republic should negotiations fail. These are hardly reassuring words for the international community, which wants the war to end quickly. Qatar has taken centre stage in mediation, with Mr Trump discussing the Iran file with the country’s emir. There is genuine reason to fear another US strike on Iran. For one, Mr Trump may want to act before January 2027, when the new Congress is empowered to scrutinise his decisions. The US government on Saturday asked its citizens in the Middle East to “exercise heightened vigilance”, while it has struck the Iranian island of Qeshm twice this week. The Iranians have not taken the bait, but have promised strong retaliation to new attacks. These developments illustrate the unpredictability of the Gulf situation: one rash move could restart the conflict, which is why mediation efforts should be stepped up. The US leadership is mistaken if it thinks that a fresh round of hostilities would be ‘limited’. If Iran does retaliate to new American or Israeli strikes, the impact of the conflict could be far more devastating than the last round. Along with needless aggression against a sovereign state, the economic shockwave caused by the conflict would hit ordinary people everywhere. In order to prevent a new military and economic crisis, the US leadership must prioritise diplomacy over war. The Iranians want an end to the blockade of their ports, as well as lifting of sanctions and the release of their funds. All these are achievable goals if the US sincerely desires peace. Even the nuclear issue can be resolved at the negotiating table if Mr Trump eschews his threatening tone. In return, Iran should promise unhindered navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. Moreover, the ceasefire must be broadened to stop the Yemen conflict as well as Israeli violence in Lebanon and the occupied Palestinian territories. Though technically, these are separate conflicts, they are also interlinked, involving Iran’s allies in the ‘Axis of Resistance’. It is decision time for Mr Trump. He can either work with regional states and negotiate an end to his own ‘forever war’. Or he can continue down the same path, with the international community paying the price for American and Israeli bellicosity. For the sake of peace, it is hoped he chooses the former option.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Bilawal’s advice
articles.content: PPP CHAIRPERSON Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari has given sound advice to the government to stop “fighting everyone”. And he did so speaking as the most important ally of the Shehbaz Sharif administration that has propped up this set-up as a major stakeholder since the controversial elections of February 2024. That is precisely why the prime minister and his PML-N should listen to him. Not that the PPP has plans to ditch him anytime soon. In the same boat, neither party has much of a choice. What appears to worry the PPP leader is the addition of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman to the list of politicians pushed into the opposition camp by recent reckless remarks against him by some cabinet ministers. The JUI-F chief was part of the PDM alliance that removed former prime minister Imran Khan. He does not accept the 2024 election results and is staunchly opposed to the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in KP. He was hardly a government ally. Yet he supported it in the passage of the recent controversial amendments to the Constitution, and consistently declined to be part of any attempt to destabilise the current system. That seems to be changing now, as the pragmatic maulana appears to be moving closer to the PTI-led opposition. Mr Bhutto-Zardari believes that such unnecessary political squabbles are diverting the government’s attention from the real problems facing the country: a stagnating economy, rising foreign-sponsored terrorism in the smaller provinces, the war in the Gulf, and more. “If we continue to fight among ourselves” and keep fighting with the PTI and Maulana Fazlur Rahman, alongside the battle against the terrorists, India, Afghanistan and others, “then they [the government] might end up remaining engaged in that [political fighting] only,” he cautioned. It is a valid point. Mr Sharif should not forget that the PTI government, too, engaged in such fights at the expense of the economy and its popularity. The PTI’s popularity had hit its lowest point before the no-confidence move was introduced. With the fallout of the Iran war putting a heavy burden on ordinary citizens, political differences should take a back seat. A government that spends its energy on feuds has little of it left to tackle more difficult challenges. The same goes for the opposition. It should also abandon its habit of putting confrontation ahead of pressing national problems.
articles.author: Editorial
